record.details: Pārvatī asks why Nala performed the vow. Himavat describes Niṣadha’s king as Veda-knowing, brave, generous, wealthy and pure, skilled with chariot, sword, arrows, bow, quiver and armour, and able to travel the three worlds. His innumerable cavalry, elephants, chariots, bowmen and weapon/fire-weapon fighters frighten Indra and direction-lords. His wife Damayantī is beautiful, virtuous and adorned; Brahmā fashioned her from selected essence and gave her the beauty of women in the three worlds. Minister Padmahasta is valiant, intelligent like Bṛhaspati, skilled in policy like Aṅgiras.
record.outcome: The king, wife, minister and capacities are introduced; comparison sages are not teachers.

record.details: Padmahasta is compared to Meru in height and the ocean in depth. A court with Apsaras dancers, praisers and brahmarṣis receives Gautama. Nala honours and seats him, calling his own birth, kingship, parents, lineage and life fruitful through the visit. Gautama says he wanted to see the king’s wealth, reports praise by Brahmā, Indra, Hari and Śiva, then asks leave. Nala pleads that he stay to remove uncertainty; the sage agrees. The king asks which merit or tapas produced his extraordinary wealth and who he was in a former birth.
record.outcome: Nala asks Gautama to explain the merit behind his wealth.

record.details: The awakened disciple bows to and embraces his compassionate guru like a son embracing his father. Mudgala honours the anthill-reemerged one as son, names him Bhṛśuṇḍi and teaches the one-syllable mantra. Verse43 connects the name with a trunk through the raw clause bhūmadhyān nirgatā śuṇḍā; its exact anatomical meaning is unresolved, and eyebrow-middle is not silently substituted. Mudgala grants excellence among sages, worship by Indra, gods, Gandharvas and Siddhas, Gaṇeśa-like sin-destroying meditation and sight, fame, fruitful sight for visitors and a lifespan of a hundred thousand kalpas by his word. Gods and Nārada’s sages visit, praise the fruitfulness of their birth, learning, parents, tapas and fame, and call him Gaṇanātha. He honours and dismisses them.
record.outcome: Mudgala gives the new name, ritual-son honour, mantra, lifespan and visitor boons.

record.details: Brahmā describes Sāma, an antyaja wrongdoer whose sight destroys piety. For wealth he murders twelve peaceful Brahmins, leaves their bodies in a cave and takes their possessions. Returning home on Māgha dark fourth at moonrise, he calls his son Gaṇeśa twice and eats with him after taking no food or water. Verse 13 explicitly says tasyaputro’sau dies that night; verse 14’s saḥ reaches Vaināyaka through the unintentional vow, and verse 16’s remaining merit produces the present Kṛtavīrya. The Sāma-versus-son death and rebirth referent is unresolved. Brahmā predicts sonbirth when sins are destroyed; the father trembles and asks another remedy.
record.outcome: Unintentional-vow merit and royal rebirth are described with a fundamental referent gap.
